analysis.one_liner: Bans large meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2017 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it sat and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meat companies sometimes own or control cattle, hogs, and other animals all the way from birth to slaughter, which critics say squeezes independent farmers who raise livestock for a living. This bill, from Senator Chuck Grassley, would have made it illegal for big meatpackers to own, feed, or effectively control livestock before slaughter, with a few exceptions for small packers, cooperatives, and animals bought shortly before processing. It was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock farmers and ranchers, who would no longer compete against the meatpackers' own company-owned feeding operations, and rural communities whose economies depend on a viable class of independent producers.

how_it_helps.text: It would make it unlawful for a packer to own or feed livestock, or to control it through arrangements that strip the farmer of real management authority, restoring a separation between meatpacking companies and the farmers who raise the animals.
Small packers owning only one plant, producer cooperatives, and short-term holdings near slaughter were exempted, aiming the rule at the largest integrated firms rather than local processors.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies such as the major beef and pork processors, which would have had to divest their livestock holdings and buy animals on the open market instead of raising them in-house.

drawbacks.text: The ban carried substantial carve-outs: it did not apply to livestock held within seven days of slaughter, to producer-owned cooperatives, to packers not required to report daily price information, or to packers owning only one processing plant, limiting how much vertical integration it would actually unwind.

Economists and packers have long argued that packer ownership of livestock lets large plants run at steady capacity and can lower processing costs; a prohibition could raise packers' costs, some of which might be passed on to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real problem — the blending of meatpacking and livestock production — with a modest design (small packers exempt, an 18-month runway for hog packers), but it had one cosponsor and never even reached a committee vote, so its costs were never fully weighed. The main cost would have fallen on large integrated meatpackers and possibly consumers through tighter packer margins; the main benefit would have accrued to independent producers.

outcome.mechanism: Grassley introduced the bill in April 2017 and it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Grassley introduced S. 813 on April 4, 2017 to amend the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921, a century-old law aimed at keeping meatpacking fair and competitive.
The bill would have prohibited packers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock to the point that the farmer no longer materially manages the operation, with limited exceptions.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry; the record shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
Only one senator, a Democrat, signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill expired with the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies keep their ability to own and control livestock, preserving the vertical integration that critics say squeezes independent farmers.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit packers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock before slaughter.

for.name: One Senate Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no other Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or a markup, keeping it from the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican lead sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, but the Senate Agriculture Committee never took it up, so no votes reveal how parties would have split.

industries.industry: Independent cattle, hog, and poultry producers (farmers and ranchers)
industries.note: The bill would have given them legal standing against packer-owned feeding operations that crowd them out and depress the prices they receive. It died, so nothing changed for them.
The packers' ability to own, feed, and vertically integrate livestock was left untouched, keeping their control over cattle and hog supply chains and the margins that come with it.

Packer ownership can smooth slaughterhouse throughput and possibly hold down some meat prices, but it also reduces the independent producers who create competitive pressure on meat markets. The bill would have tipped that balance back toward farmers, with uncertain effects at the grocery counter.
